**The Inventory**

My grandmother kept a drawer of rubber bands. Not a few—hundreds, thick and thin, some so old they'd gone brittle and snapped if you stretched them, some still supple, blue from the broccoli, red from the newspaper, the wide beige ones that came around bundles of mail. She never threw one away. When she died and we cleaned out the house, my mother stood over that drawer for a long time, and then she scooped the whole tangle into a grocery bag and put it in her own purse, and as far as I know she still has it.

I've been thinking about what people keep. Not the things they mean to keep—the photographs, the rings, the letters tied with ribbon—but the things that accumulate without a decision ever being made. The drawer of rubber bands. The mug of dead pens. The single glove waiting for its partner to come home.

There's a man I used to see every morning at the bus stop on Carlton Street. He carried a plastic bag from a hardware store that closed in 2009, and I never once saw him put anything into it or take anything out. He held it the way you'd hold a hand. I don't know his name. I moved, and then I stopped taking that bus, and I have no idea whether he still stands there or whether the bag finally gave out or whether he did. But I think about him more than I think about some people I've known for years, and I don't entirely understand why. Maybe because he was a question I never asked.

Here is a thing I've noticed: the mind is also a drawer of rubber bands. You don't choose what stays. You'd like to keep the afternoon your father taught you to whistle, and instead you keep the pattern of the linoleum in the kitchen where it happened, the exact yellow of it, the way one tile was cracked in the corner near the stove. You'd like to keep what your friend said to you the last time you spoke, and instead you keep the sound of the ice machine in the hallway of the hotel where she was staying. The mind is not a curator. It's a kid at the beach picking up whatever shell is closest.

I read once that the word "souvenir" in French just means "to remember." It's a verb before it's a noun. You don't buy a souvenir; you souvenir. The snow globe is incidental. What you're really carrying home is the act of having been somewhere and wanting proof.

My grandmother's rubber bands were proof of something too, though I'm not sure what. That mail had arrived. That vegetables had been bought and eaten. That a life had been made of ordinary deliveries, one after another, for eighty-some years. Maybe she kept them because throwing them away felt like saying the day they arrived hadn't mattered. Or maybe she just grew up in a time when you didn't throw anything away, and the habit outlived the reason. Habits do that. They're the rubber bands of behavior—stretched around something once, then left on long after the bundle has been opened.

I have a habit of touching doorframes when I leave a room. I don't know where it came from. I've asked my family and nobody else does it. It's not superstition, exactly—I don't think anything bad will happen if I don't—but I feel a small incompleteness, like a sentence without a period. I've been doing it, I think, since I was about seven. That's a lot of doorframes. If each touch left a mark, you could trace the whole map of my life in fingerprints at shoulder height.

What I'm circling toward, I think, is this: we like to imagine we are the sum of our decisions. The career we chose, the person we married, the city we moved to. But I suspect we're at least as much the sum of what we failed to decide about. The things that stayed because we never got around to removing them. The routes we walk because we walked them once. The people who remain vivid because we never asked the question that would have resolved them into someone ordinary.

There's a kind of tenderness in this, if you let there be. The undecided parts of a life are the parts that weren't performed. Nobody keeps rubber bands to impress anyone. Nobody touches a doorframe for an audience. These are the gestures we make when we think no one is watching, including ourselves, and so they're maybe the truest record of who we actually are, as opposed to who we've arranged to seem.

When my mother took that bag of rubber bands, I thought it was grief doing something irrational. Now I think she was just recognizing an heirloom when she saw one. The good china was for company. The rubber bands were for my grandmother, only and always, a private ledger of days kept without anyone having to know she was keeping it.

I hope somebody, someday, stands over one of my drawers and doesn't know what to do with it. I hope there's something in there that makes no sense and can't be explained and clearly mattered anyway. I hope they take it home in their purse.

The man at the bus stop—I want to say one more thing about him. Once, in the rain, I saw him lift the plastic bag over his head, not to shield himself, just to keep it dry. He stood there getting soaked, holding this empty bag up like a lantern. I remember thinking it was the saddest thing I'd ever seen. Now I'm not so sure. Now I think it might have been one of the clearest examples of love I've witnessed: keeping something safe long past the point where anyone could tell you why.
